lessons.title: Require equality before comparing generic values
lessons.summary: Implement sameEnds for empty, singleton, matching and different endpoints; preserve the input.
explanation: A generic parameter names a type chosen at each call. A constraint says which operations that type must support. Equatable promises equality comparison; it does not make every pair equal.

sameEnds accepts an array whose elements share one type T and returns Bool. The where clause T: Equatable permits == inside the body; <T: Equatable> is another spelling of this single constraint. first and last are optional endpoints; guard unwraps both or returns false for an empty array. This reads the array without changing it. A one-element array has equal endpoints. print sends the returned value to standard output.

```swift
func sameEnds<T>(_ values: [T]) -> Bool where T: Equatable {
    guard let first = values.first, let last = values.last else {
        return false
    }
    return first == last
}
print(sameEnds([4, 9, 4]))
print(sameEnds(["oak", "elm"]))
```
Expected output:
```text
true
false
```

```swift
    guard let first = values.first, let last = values.last else {
        return false
    }
    return first == last
}
print(sameEnds([Int]()))
print(sameEnds(["ash"]))
```
Expected output:
```text

true
```

lessons.title: Match associated types across two conformers
lessons.summary: Implement pair so both items survive in input order.
explanation: An associated type is a type slot declared by a protocol. Each conforming type supplies what that slot means. Two different conforming types can share the same item type.

ItemSource requires a readable item and names its type Item. Box<Value> infers Item from its stored item: Value. The automatically supplied Box(item:) initializer stores its argument. CountSource is a different conforming struct whose item is always Int; CountSource(item:) stores that Int. Box<Int> and CountSource are different source types with the same Item. pair accepts two possibly different source types A and B, but where A.Item == B.Item requires the same associated type, not equal item values. It returns an array containing the first then second item. [A.Item] is an array type whose element type is that shared item type.

lessons.title: Keep successful optional transformations
lessons.summary: Parse valid whole numbers, retaining zero, duplicates and source order.
explanation: compactMap calls a transformation for each element and keeps its non-nil results. It does not discard zero, false or empty text merely because they look empty.

parsedNumbers takes strings and returns the successful Int parses in source order. Int(text) is a failable integer conversion: malformed or unrepresentable text gives nil. The closure text in names each input; its last expression is its optional Int result. texts.compactMap unwraps successful results into [Int], omitting nil. It does not mutate texts or remove duplicate successful values.

```swift
func parsedNumbers(_ texts: [String]) -> [Int] {
    return texts.compactMap { text in
        Int(text)
    }
}
let source = ["8", "bad", "0", "8"]
print(parsedNumbers(source))
print(source)
```
Expected output:
```text
[8, 0, 8]
["8", "bad", "0", "8"]
```

```swift

    return texts.compactMap { text in

    }
}
print(parsedNumbers(["-3", "no", "2"]))
print(parsedNumbers([]))
```
Expected output:
```text

[]
```

lessons.title: Start a reduction with an explicit accumulator
lessons.summary: Return the prefix followed by every bracketed label, including duplicate and empty labels.
explanation: reduce turns a sequence into one result by repeatedly combining the result so far with the next element. The initial accumulator is already a real result: an empty sequence returns it unchanged.

joinedLabels takes labels plus a prefix. labels.reduce(prefix) starts the accumulated String at prefix. Each closure call receives that string and one label, then returns a new string with the label in brackets. + concatenates strings here; it is not integer addition. The next call receives the returned accumulator. reduce does not mutate labels or prefix, and source order matters for this string-building operation.

```swift
func joinedLabels(_ labels: [String], startingWith prefix: String) -> String {
    return labels.reduce(prefix) { accumulated, label in
        accumulated + "[" + label + "]"
    }
}
print(joinedLabels(["map", "notes"], startingWith: "Trip:"))
```
Expected output:
```text
Trip:[map][notes]
```

lessons.title: Join a fixed pair of child tasks
lessons.summary: Keep both child results in the sum and preserve terminal cleanup on failure.
explanation: async let creates a child task whose lifetime is bounded by its surrounding scope. Reading its result needs await; a throwing result also needs try. Leaving the scope waits for unfinished children, requesting cancellation when required rather than forcibly stopping arbitrary code.

compute creates two children before awaiting their sum. CompletionLog is an actor: calls from outside cross its isolation boundary with await; item contains no suspension and actor access is serialized. The tiny jobs therefore demonstrate lifetime, not parallel speed. item returns its supplied Int or throws; defer increments finished whenever that call exits, including its throwing path. count reads the finished total. joined awaits compute to terminal completion and returns a named tuple with an optional value and completion count. On a failure, scope cleanup has joined both children before the outer catch reads the log. These jobs do not check cancellation, so both still finish; this is not a cancellation-performance guarantee.

lessons.title: Collect a variable number of child results
lessons.summary: Return every word length exactly once, sorted, including zero and duplicate lengths.
explanation: A task group creates one structured scope for a number of child tasks chosen at runtime. Its result sequence arrives in completion order, which need not be input order.

withTaskGroup receives the child result type Int.self and the body result type [Int].self; .self here names a type value, not an instance. group.addTask starts a child closure returning one word’s Character count. Each child captures one immutable String value; no child mutates lengths. The parent consumes each result with for await and append adds it to the array. sorted returns an ascending copy, making the output order deliberate while preserving duplicates. Empty input creates no children and returns []. All children finish before the group scope exits. This example neither promises speed nor demonstrates cancellation; cancellation in Swift is cooperative, not thread killing.

lessons.title: Export an API across a real module boundary
lessons.summary: Explain and optionally reproduce the complete local workflow; this lesson has no in-app executable checks.
explanation: A module is a separately compiled unit with an API visible to its clients. public declarations can cross that boundary; default internal declarations stay within the module. private further restricts access to the enclosing declaration and its same-file extensions.

Use an existing Swift 6.0-or-newer command-line toolchain and a new empty local directory for each variant. These are complete local files, not one source file for the app’s Run button. Actual recorded execution is Swift 6.4.1/Linux in language mode 6, not a Mac/Xcode or compiler 6.0 verification. No registry package, network service or user-machine installation is needed. Commands below assume a shell with swift/swiftc on PATH; preserve paths and run from that directory. RouteLabel is public, but that alone does not export its initializer or methods: those also say public. RouteLabel(prefix:) stores a prefix, and text(for:) combines that stored value with a place into a String. private prefix is hidden; internalTag omits an access modifier and is internal. -module-name names the compiled library module; -emit-module writes its importable interface and -emit-object writes linkable code. -parse-as-library treats this file as library declarations. The client uses import RouteKit; -I . finds the module here and RouteKit.o supplies its implementation when linking. This compiles two modules without a package or dynamic-library search path.

File `RouteKit.swift`:
```swift
public struct RouteLabel {
    private let prefix: String
    let internalTag = "local"
    public init(prefix: String) {
        self.prefix = prefix
    }
    public func text(for place: String) -> String {
        return prefix + ":" + place
    }
}
```

File `main.swift`:
```swift
import RouteKit
let label = RouteLabel(prefix: "Walk")
print(label.text(for: "Pond"))
```

Run these local commands in order:
```sh
swiftc -swift-version 6 -emit-module -emit-object -parse-as-library -module-name RouteKit RouteKit.swift -o RouteKit.o
swiftc -swift-version 6 -I . main.swift RouteKit.o -o demo
./demo
```
The final command prints exactly `Walk:Pond` followed by a newline. Build commands must succeed first.

Run `swift test`. The function is ordinary code, not a discovered test: there is no @Test annotation. Inspect the Swift Testing count, not merely process exit status or an XCTest compatibility summary; the observed Swift 6.4.1 Linux run exits 0 and says `0 tests in 0 suites passed`. That is an empty run, not a pass for prefixesPlace. Other toolchain versions may format or handle empty discovery differently.

lessons.title: Separate a compiler rejection from a wrong answer
lessons.summary: Repair the OR logic bug using an inclusive interval contract; test both endpoints and both outside sides.
explanation: A compiler error prevents a program from becoming an executable. A logic error can compile normally and still violate the intended contract. Reduce a problem to a small complete example, then compare expected and actual behavior.

isWithin takes an Int and inclusive lower/upper Int bounds, returning Bool. >= and <= test the two boundaries; && requires both. For a reversed interval no value satisfies both comparisons. This function does not need subtraction, so extreme Int values are safe to compare. A quoted string is not automatically an Int argument: fix the type mismatch rather than hiding it. After compilation succeeds, test boundaries and outside values; one happy-path call does not prove the condition is right.

```swift
func isWithin(_ value: Int, lower: Int, upper: Int) -> Bool {
    return value >= lower && value <= upper
}
print(isWithin(5, lower: 2, upper: 8))
print(isWithin(2, lower: 2, upper: 8))
```
Expected output:
```text
true
true
```

```swift
func isWithin(_ value: Int, lower: Int, upper: Int) -> Bool {
    return value >= lower && value <= upper
}
print(isWithin(9, lower: 2, upper: 8))
print(isWithin(5, lower: 8, upper: 2))
```
Expected output:
```text
false
false
```

This separate complete local example is intentionally rejected. It is author-validated compiler evidence, not an additional learner Run checks feature.
```swift
func isWithin(_ value: Int, lower: Int, upper: Int) -> Bool {
    return value >= lower && value <= upper
}
print(isWithin("5", lower: 2, upper: 8))
```
The intended diagnostic identifies cannot convert value of type 'String' to expected argument type 'Int'. Do not paste it together with a success example.
